needs.title: Child restraint positioning

source_cards.front: What must every child restraint system made since January one, one thousand nine hundred eighty-one, be designed to do, and what label does it carry?
source_cards.back: Every child restraint system made since January one, nineteen eighty-one, must be designed to pass demanding safety tests and carries a label giving its manufacture date and its conformity with federal safety standards.

source_cards.front: Which way must an infant seat never face, and what does the seat label show?
source_cards.back: An infant seat must never be turned to face forward, and the seat label shows the child size and weight it is designed to protect.

source_cards.front: According to the manual, how must children under age two, and those under thirty pounds, ride?
source_cards.back: The manual says children under age two and those weighing under thirty pounds must ride in a rear-facing child restraint equipped with a five-point harness.

source_cards.front: How must children under age eight who are shorter than fifty-seven inches ride?
source_cards.back: Children under age eight and shorter than fifty-seven inches (four feet, nine inches) must ride in a rear seat, either in a forward-facing restraint with a five-point harness until they outgrow it and then a booster seat, or in a booster seat.

source_cards.front: Where must all children under age eight sit, and when may they ride up front?
source_cards.back: All children under age eight must sit in a rear seat, and only a vehicle with no rear seat allows them to ride in an approved restraint or booster seat up front.

source_cards.front: Where may a rear-facing child restraint never be placed?
source_cards.back: A rear-facing child restraint may never be placed in a front seat that has a passenger-side air bag that has not been disabled or turned off.

source_cards.front: Where and how should an infant ride in a vehicle that has air bags?
source_cards.back: An infant should always ride in a rear-facing infant safety seat in the back seat of a vehicle that has air bags.

needs.title: Following and stopping distance

source_cards.front: Which factors does stopping distance depend on?
source_cards.back: Stopping distance depends on the driver's reaction time, weather and visibility, vehicle weight, brake condition, tire type and condition, the road surface and speed.

source_cards.front: What does the stopping table give for a vehicle at ten miles per hour?
source_cards.back: The manual's stopping table gives a total of nineteen feet at ten miles per hour, made up of eleven feet of reaction distance and eight feet of braking distance.

source_cards.front: What does the stopping table give for a vehicle at twenty miles per hour?
source_cards.back: The manual's stopping table gives a total of fifty-three feet at twenty miles per hour, made up of twenty-two feet of reaction distance and thirty-one feet of braking distance.

source_cards.front: What does the stopping table give for a vehicle at thirty miles per hour?
source_cards.back: The manual's stopping table gives a total of one hundred two feet at thirty miles per hour, made up of thirty-three feet of reaction distance and sixty-nine feet of braking distance.

source_cards.front: What does the stopping table give for a vehicle at fifty miles per hour?
source_cards.back: The manual's stopping table gives a total of two hundred forty-seven feet at fifty miles per hour, made up of fifty-five feet of reaction distance and one hundred ninety-two feet of braking distance.

source_cards.front: What does the stopping table give for a vehicle at sixty miles per hour?
source_cards.back: The manual's stopping table gives a total of three hundred forty-three feet at sixty miles per hour, made up of sixty-six feet of reaction distance and two hundred seventy-seven feet of braking distance.

source_cards.front: What does the stopping table give for a vehicle at seventy miles per hour?
source_cards.back: The manual's stopping table gives a total of four hundred fifty-three feet at seventy miles per hour, made up of seventy-seven feet of reaction distance and three hundred seventy-six feet of braking distance.

source_cards.front: When may a hand come off the steering wheel?
source_cards.back: Both hands should stay on the wheel at all times except while shifting gears or giving hand signals.

source_cards.front: What is the driver's hand signal for stopping or slowing down?
source_cards.back: The hand signal for stopping or slowing down is the arm extended downward with the palm facing the rear.

source_cards.front: What is the driver's hand signal for a right turn?
source_cards.back: The hand signal for a right turn is the arm extended upward.

source_cards.front: What is the driver's hand signal for a left turn?
source_cards.back: The hand signal for a left turn is the arm held straight out.

source_cards.front: How do the three driver hand signals differ from each other?
source_cards.back: The three driver hand signals are easy to mix up: arm down with the palm to the rear means stop or slow, arm up means a right turn, and arm straight out means a left turn.

source_cards.front: What extra right-turn signal may bicyclists, skateboarders and inline skaters use?

source_cards.front: Before a turn, what comes first, and what comes second?
source_cards.back: Signal first, with the turn signal or a hand signal, and only then move into the proper lane for the turn.

needs.title: Crosswalks and stop positions

source_cards.front: What must a driver do for a pedestrian in a marked crosswalk or at an unmarked crosswalk at an intersection?
source_cards.back: A driver must come to a full stop, not merely slow or yield, for a pedestrian in a marked crosswalk or one crossing at an unmarked crosswalk at an intersection.

source_cards.front: If the signal changes to Don't Walk while a pedestrian is still in the crosswalk, what do you do?
source_cards.back: Stop for every pedestrian still in a crosswalk even if the signal has changed to Don't Walk.

source_cards.front: What two things must you never do around a crosswalk?
source_cards.back: Never overtake a vehicle that has stopped at a crosswalk for a pedestrian, and never block or park in a crosswalk.

source_cards.front: Besides walkers, who else must you yield to at crosswalks and intersections?
source_cards.back: Yield to people using motorized or mobility-assistance devices in a crosswalk or trying to cross, and to other vehicles already inside the intersection.

source_cards.front: At a stop sign, where must you stop and when may you go on?
source_cards.back: At a stop sign, come to a complete stop within five feet of the nearest crosswalk or stop line, then enter only after yielding to pedestrians and to any traffic close enough to be an immediate hazard.

source_cards.front: When turning left, who must you yield to and stop for?
source_cards.back: When turning left, yield to oncoming traffic and stop for pedestrians in the crosswalk.

needs.title: Freeway entry and exit

source_cards.front: What are highways, parkways and turnpikes like, and who yields when you enter them?
source_cards.back: Highways, parkways and turnpikes are divided roads with speeds up to sixty-five miles per hour and no direct intersections, entered by an acceleration lane, and drivers must yield to traffic already on the main road.

source_cards.front: What should you do as you leave the acceleration lane to enter a highway?
source_cards.back: When entering a highway, speed up to the flow of traffic as you leave the acceleration lane and avoid stopping completely in that lane.

source_cards.front: What should you do if you miss your highway exit?
source_cards.back: If you miss an exit, continue to the next one, and never back up on an exit ramp or deceleration lane.

source_cards.front: How does an acceleration lane differ from a deceleration lane?
source_cards.back: An acceleration lane is for speeding up and should not be stopped in, while a deceleration lane is where you start slowing down and obey its advisory speed.

source_cards.front: On which side are most exit ramps, and what do you do when an exit is on the left?
source_cards.back: Most exit ramps and deceleration lanes are on the right; when an exit is on the left, follow the signs that direct traffic to the proper exit lane.

source_cards.front: In a weave lane, which driver must yield?
source_cards.back: In a weave lane, which serves as both an entrance and an exit, the driver coming from the entrance ramp must yield to the driver leaving the expressway.

source_cards.front: Which vehicles re-entering the flow of traffic get the right-of-way?
source_cards.back: Buses and postal vehicles re-entering the flow of traffic are given the right-of-way.

source_cards.front: What must you do at a yield sign?
source_cards.back: At a yield sign, slow down and give the right-of-way to traffic on the crossing road, stopping if needed.

source_cards.front: How does the multi-way stop rule differ from the yield sign rule?
source_cards.back: A multi-way stop gives the right-of-way to the driver on the right when two arrive together, while a yield sign requires slowing and giving way to the crossing road's traffic.

source_cards.front: How do you treat a traffic signal that is dark because of a power failure?
source_cards.back: A traffic signal that is dark because of a power failure or other malfunction is treated as a four-way stop.

source_cards.front: As a general rule at an uncontrolled intersection, which vehicle yields?
source_cards.back: As a general rule at an uncontrolled intersection, the vehicle on the left yields to the vehicle on the right.

source_cards.front: What decides the right-of-way in a New Jersey traffic circle?
source_cards.back: New Jersey has no set rules for traffic circles: the circle's established flow pattern usually decides the right-of-way, a major highway running through it usually dominates, and stop or yield signs at the entrances also govern.

source_cards.front: When right-of-way in a traffic circle is unclear, what rule do you fall back on?
source_cards.back: When it is unclear who has the right-of-way in a traffic circle, fall back on the basic uncontrolled-intersection rule: the vehicle on the left yields to the vehicle approaching from the right.

source_cards.back: When one center line is broken, passing is allowed only from the side with the broken line.

source_cards.front: How do you read center line markings for passing?
source_cards.back: Center line markings read from your own side: two solid lines forbid passing, a broken line on your side permits it, and two broken lines permit it from both sides.

source_cards.front: On which side do you normally pass, and when is passing on the right permitted?
source_cards.back: Passing is normally done on the left; passing on the right is permitted only where the road has more than one lane in your direction and traffic is moving in two or more steady lines, or where the driver ahead is turning left and there is room.

source_cards.front: Is passing on the right shoulder of the road ever allowed?
source_cards.back: Passing on the right shoulder of the road is never allowed and is against the law.

source_cards.front: For a left turn from a two-way road onto a four-lane highway, which lane do you turn into?
source_cards.back: For a left turn from a two-way road onto a four-lane highway, turn into the lane nearest the center line, which is the passing lane, and move right out of it when traffic allows.

source_cards.front: Which railroad warnings are passive and which are active?

source_cards.front: How much legal force do road markings carry?
source_cards.back: Road markings carry the same force of law as signs and traffic signals.

source_cards.front: What do yellow center lines separate, and what do white lines separate?
source_cards.back: Yellow center lines separate traffic moving in opposite directions, while white lines separate lanes moving the same way and mark road edges.

source_cards.front: What does a dashed line on your side of the center line mean, and a solid one?
source_cards.back: A dashed line on your side of the center line means you may pass when it is safe, and a solid line on your side means you may not pass.

source_cards.front: With a solid and a dashed yellow line side by side, when may you pass?
source_cards.back: With a solid yellow line and a dashed yellow line side by side, pass only when the dashed line is on your side, and finish the pass before the dashes turn solid.

source_cards.front: What do double solid lines mean for passing?
source_cards.back: Double solid yellow and white lines prohibit passing, so never cross a solid yellow line to pass, stay in your lane and keep right when driving slowly.

source_cards.front: What do road arrows and white dashed lines tell drivers?
source_cards.back: Road arrows used with other signs show the direction a driver must take from that lane, and white dashed lines separate lanes on multi-lane highways.

source_cards.front: What do edge lines mark?
source_cards.back: Edge lines separate the shoulder from the travel lane and mark the edge of the highway, and yellow edge lines do the same job.

source_cards.front: Where do you stop when there is no stop line, and where when there is one?
source_cards.back: Where no stop line is painted, stop before the crosswalk when a sign, signal or pedestrian requires you to stop, and where a white stop line exists, stop at it.

source_cards.front: What do white special pavement markings such as STOP AHEAD alert drivers to?
source_cards.back: White special pavement markings such as STOP AHEAD, SCHOOL and RXR alert drivers to special conditions ahead.

needs.title: Traffic and pedestrian signals

source_cards.front: Who wins when a police officer directing traffic and the traffic signal disagree?
source_cards.back: A police officer directing traffic can overrule the traffic signals, and a driver must always obey law enforcement orders and directions.

source_cards.front: In what order are the lights on a vertical signal, and where is red on a horizontal one?
source_cards.back: On a vertical signal, red is always on top, yellow in the middle and green third, with any green arrow at the bottom; on a horizontal signal, red is always on the left.

source_cards.front: What must you do at a steady red light?
source_cards.back: At a red light, stop before the intersection or crosswalk and stay stopped until the light turns green.

source_cards.front: What does a steady yellow light require?
source_cards.back: At a steady yellow light, stop before entering the intersection or crosswalk unless you are too close to stop safely.

source_cards.front: What does a yellow arrow warn you about?
source_cards.back: A yellow arrow warns that the light is about to go from green to red, giving you time to stop safely.

source_cards.front: On a green light, whom must you still yield to, and what extra yield applies before a left turn?
source_cards.back: On a green light, go ahead but yield to pedestrians and vehicles still in the intersection, and before turning left yield to oncoming vehicles.

source_cards.front: What does a green arrow allow, alone or with a red light?
source_cards.back: A green arrow, alone or together with a red light, lets you go only in the direction the arrow points, while still yielding to pedestrians.

source_cards.front: What does a flashing yellow light mean?
source_cards.back: A flashing yellow light means slow down and proceed with care.

source_cards.front: What does a flashing red light require?
source_cards.back: A flashing red light means stop, yield to traffic and pedestrians, and go only when it is safe.

source_cards.front: How does a flashing yellow light differ from a flashing red light?
source_cards.back: A flashing yellow light only asks you to slow down and take care, but a flashing red light requires a full stop before going on when safe.

source_cards.front: How much legal force do road markings carry?
source_cards.back: Road markings carry the same force of law as signs and traffic signals.
